notes.meaning: When Ish-bosheth heard that his general Abner was dead, his courage failed him completely. Abner had been the real strength propping up his weak rule. The people of Israel were thrown into confusion and fear, not knowing what would happen next.

Ish-bosheth had two captains who led raiding troops, named Baanah and Rechab. They belonged to the tribe of Benjamin, which was Saul's own tribe. Their home city of Beeroth was counted as part of Benjamin's territory.

The original people of Beeroth had run away to Gittaim and lived there as foreigners. They likely fled when the Philistines swept through the area after Saul's defeat. Even though the people lived elsewhere, their roots were still tied to Benjamin.

Saul's son Jonathan had a son named Mephibosheth, who could not walk. When news of Saul and Jonathan's deaths reached his home, his nurse panicked and dropped him while trying to run away. This note shows that Saul's royal family had no capable heir left to claim the throne.

Baanah and Rechab traveled to Ish-bosheth's home in Mahanaim around the middle of the day. In that hot climate, it was common for people, including kings, to rest during the noontime heat. Ish-bosheth was resting on his couch, leaving himself completely unguarded.

The two brothers walked into the inner rooms pretending they were there to get wheat rations for their soldiers. Because officers routinely collected grain from royal storehouses, no one suspected them. They caught the king asleep and fatally stabbed him in the stomach.

After stabbing Ish-bosheth in his bedroom, the killers cut off his head to take as proof of the deed. They slipped away and fled through the Jordan Valley under cover of darkness. They traveled all night to carry their grim trophy south to David at Hebron.

The brothers presented Ish-bosheth's head to David, calling the dead king an enemy who had hunted David's life. They claimed the Lord had worked through them to avenge David against Saul's house. They fully expected a generous reward for clearing David's way to the throne.

David replied with a solemn oath in the name of the living God, who had rescued him from every trouble. He made it clear that he did not need murder or evil deeds to win his kingdom. David trusted God alone, not human treachery, to fulfill His promises.

David pointed back to the messenger who had come to Ziklag boasting about King Saul's death. That man expected a great reward for bringing what he thought was good news. Instead, David had executed him for claiming to strike down God's chosen king.

David told the two brothers that their crime was far worse than the Amalekite's. They had murdered an innocent man who had done them no harm, inside his own home and while he slept. David declared that justice demanded their lives to rid the land of their bloodguilt.

David ordered his guards to execute Rechab and Baanah and cut off their hands and feet. Their bodies were hung by the public pool in Hebron as a solemn warning against murder and as proof that David had no part in the plot. Meanwhile, David gave Ish-bosheth's head an honorable burial in Abner's tomb.
